chapters.title: I Lost A Bet To A Penny
The Office That Picks The Last Digit
The Store That Told The Truth

beats.text: Look at this price tag for one second. Be honest. Your brain just said three hundred something. Didn't it?
It's four hundred dollars. And stores have been running that one penny trick on you for over a hundred years.
Your brain got robbed by one cent.
By the end of this video you'll see this exact tag again and your brain will finally read it right. And it takes one tiny habit.
But most people scroll away before that part. Which is exactly what the pricing guys are counting on.
So let me tell you how I lost twenty dollars to my neighbor Bob.
I walk out of a store feeling very smart. Because I'm sure this ninety nine stuff only works on other people.
Me thinking I'm immune to nine ninety nine.
Bob grins and says twenty bucks says you can't tell me what you just spent without looking at the receipt.
Easy. Headphones. A lamp. A frying pan. Some snacks. About ninety bucks.
The receipt says one hundred twenty four dollars and ninety five cents.
Bob with my twenty dollars.
I didn't forget anything. My brain kept the first digit of every price and threw the rest away. Like a guy who reads the first word of your text and replies okay.
And before you laugh at me look at this shelf tag. Is your gut saying three bucks or four?
Now three at once. You've got three seconds. Add them up in your head. No calculator.
If you got somewhere around ninety congratulations. You're me. The real total is three cents short of a hundred.
Everyone who just did the math.
So I'm out twenty dollars and I want to know how a trick this dumb beat me. And the trail starts in an Ohio bar in eighteen seventy nine.
A bar owner in Dayton named James Ritty was sure his bartenders were stealing from him.
So he invented a machine he called the Incorruptible Cashier. You know it as the cash register.
And here's the legend. If your drink costs one round dollar the bartender can slide that bill into his pocket. At ninety nine cents he has to open the drawer for your penny.
The bartender when the drink costs ninety nine cents.
Great story. It's all over the internet. But nobody ever found a shop owner from back then saying that's why he did it.
There's another legend about a Chicago newspaper man named Melville Stone who sold his paper for one penny. Supposedly shops priced things one cent under so you'd get a penny back for his paper.
Except someone dug through that paper's old ads and prices ending in nine were rare back then. So I lost twenty bucks to a rumor.
Nobody knows who started the ninety nine. But we know why it never stopped. And that part happens inside your head.
So let's test your brain on something that isn't even a price. Look at the miles on this used truck.
Ninety nine thousand miles feels a lot younger than a hundred thousand right? The gap is one long weekend of driving.
Economists looked at millions of used car sales. A car sold just under a big round mileage number went for about two hundred dollars more than the same car just over it.
Car buyers at ninety nine thousand miles versus a hundred thousand.
Here's what's going on. You read from left to right. And your brain decides how big a number is before your eyes reach the end. Scientists call it the left digit effect.
Researchers at New York University tested it. Two ninety nine felt way cheaper than three dollars. But when the first digit stayed the same that one cent did almost nothing.
And I do this with everything. I'm thirty nine years and eleven months old and I tell people I'm thirty something.
Me at thirty nine and eleven months.
Now guess with me. When a price climbs one cent from four ninety nine to five dollars how many cents does that feel like to shoppers? Put your number in the comments.
While you think about it I found a man who built a whole empire on those two little nines. His name was Dave Gold. Great name.
Gold ran a little liquor store in Los Angeles. When he put wine on sale for a dollar and two cents it just sat there. At ninety eight cents it sat there too.
But when he wrote ninety nine cents on the sign it was gone in no time. He called it a magic number.
Read that again. The wine sold better at ninety nine cents than at ninety eight. A higher price beat a lower one just because of how it looked.
My brain reading prices.
So he opened a store where everything cost ninety nine cents. It grew into hundreds of stores. And when costs went up the new price was ninety nine point nine nine cents.
And he wasn't alone. Steve Jobs priced every song in his new music store at ninety nine cents. It sold a million songs in the first week.
Apple deciding song prices.
And now I wanted to know who decides my lamp costs nineteen ninety nine and not twenty. Because somebody does.
Every big chain has a pricing office. Choosing the last digit is somebody's actual job. With a spreadsheet.
Somebody at a store literally gets paid to pick the nine. Imagine telling your mom that's your job.
Economists checked eight years of prices from a big supermarket. Nine was the most common last digit of all.

And here's your answer. A researcher tracked thousands of products in twenty five store chains. When a price goes from four ninety nine to five dollars shoppers react like it went up about twenty cents.
One penny hits your brain like twenty of them. So a store that knocks off one cent gets treated like it gave you a real discount.
Stores finding out one cent feels like twenty.
Want proof it prints money? Economists ran a test on twenty one million riders of the ride app Lyft.
About half of everything a cheaper fare did happened at the moment the price slipped under a round dollar. Worth around one hundred sixty million dollars a year to them.
So who wins? Not one evil guy in a tower. A quiet office with a spreadsheet. Using a glitch inside your own head.
Think about how many prices you see in one week. Groceries and gas and apps and rent and that little snack at the counter. Every single one gets the same tiny haircut in your head.
And if you think one cent is the smallest thing they'd shave off wait until you look at a gas station sign.
See the tiny number next to the price? That's nine tenths of a cent. There's no coin in your pocket for that.
It started in the nineteen thirties when gas taxes came in slivers of a cent. The taxes changed. The nine tenths never left.
On one tank it's about a dime. But Americans burn so much gas that the invisible fraction adds up to more than a billion dollars a year.
Me paying for a coin that doesn't exist.
So I had one hopeful thought. If we all hate being tricked then a store that stops doing it should win. One huge company tried exactly that.
In twenty eleven J C Penney hired a new boss. Ron Johnson. The guy who built the Apple Store.
His new company was running five hundred ninety different sales in a single year. So he cut the sales. Killed the coupons. And every price ended in a nice honest zero.
Be honest with me. You'd love a store like that. Right?
Shoppers walked away. Sales fell by about four billion dollars in one year. A quarter of the whole business.
Shoppers seeing honest prices at J C Penney.
Johnson was out after seventeen months. The coupons came right back. And here's the ugly truth. The stores aren't forcing this on us. We punish the honest price.
We reward the pretty price and punish the honest one.
And then America stopped making the penny. The last ones were made in Philadelphia in November twenty twenty five.
Each penny cost almost four cents to make. Which is a very strange way to run a one cent coin.
So the ninety nine should be dead. Right? Nope. Stores can round your cash total to the nearest nickel. But tap your card and you still pay nine ninety nine.
And the tag on the shelf still says nine ninety nine. The coin died and the trick didn't even blink.
The ninety nine after the penny died.
But then I noticed something. The trick only works in the first second while your brain is on autopilot. So what if I grab the wheel? Quick reminder this is education and not advice.
Rule one. I say every price out loud and round it up. Nineteen ninety nine is twenty. The cashier thinks I'm weird. I do not care.
It sounds silly. But it forces your brain to read the whole number and not just the first digit.
Rule two. I keep a running total in round numbers while I shop. No more mystery receipts.
Rule three. One question. Would I still want this at the round price? If the lamp is a yes at nineteen ninety nine and a no at twenty then I never wanted the lamp. I wanted the nine.
Me now at every checkout.
Then I knocked on Bob's door. Double or nothing. He watched me shop. I muttered round numbers the whole way like a man counting sheep. At the exit I said one hundred ten dollars.
The receipt said one hundred nine dollars and ninety four cents. Bob paid up. I got my twenty back and twenty more on top.
Bob handing me forty dollars.
Now it's your turn. Here's the exact tag from the first second of this video. Read it out loud. Round it up.
Four hundred dollars. If that's the first thing your brain said then the trick just stopped working on you.
The price isn't nineteen ninety nine. It's twenty. It was always twenty.
Oh and I finally said my real age out loud too. I'm forty. I took it pretty well.
Next time a very friendly guy at the phone store offers me a brand new phone for free. That should worry you.
Subscribe. It costs zero dollars. Not zero ninety nine. Zero.
